## PDF page 100

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/GTO/Poker-Math-Preflop-Workbook.pdf#page=100)

```text
                       MAKING BETS


It is also important to understand that your opponent gets pot odds whenever
you bet or raise. By thinking ahead and considering the pot odds your bet
size would offer your opponent, you can be proactive in offering them unfa-
vorable pot odds – whether you are bluffing or value betting.

Each page contains two exercises where you are given the pot size before
you bet. Complete the table below as if you were to bet for each of the listed
sizes. Jot down what percentage of the pot your bet represents, their pot
odds as a ratio, and their equity requirement when facing that bet size.




Once again, pay special attention to how the bet size, as a percentage of the
pot, correlates with the pot odds ratio and equity requirement.

GLGL.

                                  PA G E 1 0 0
```

## PDF page 104

[Open source PDF](../../../../sources/pdf/GTO/Poker-Math-Preflop-Workbook.pdf#page=104)

```text
                                    RAISES


Pot odds exist when making and facing bets, but they also exist when making
and facing raises. Everything that you have done so far to calculate the pot
odds ratio and equity requirement is the same, but there are two new details
to factor in:

   1. When facing raises, remember that any money you previously
      invested no longer belongs to you. If you bet $20 into $50 and then
      face a raise to $65 total, your call would risk $45 to win $135.

   2. The percentage of the pot that a raise represents is based upon the
      “3x + original pot” rule. To make a pot-sized raise you just take:

                (3 * YOU R OPP ON E N T ’ S B E T ) + T H E OR IG I NA L P O T


      Where the “original pot” is all the money in before your opponent’s last
      bet or call. So if the pot is $150 and your opponent bets $100, to make a
      pot-sized raise you would do (3*$100)+$150 and throw out $450 total.

      A pot-sized bet/raise always gives your opponent 2:1 pot odds, and in
      this example your opponent would need to call $350 to win $700, giving
      them exactly 2:1 and proving that you pot-sized everything correctly.

Each page contains two exercises where you are given the pot size before
you raise or face a raise. Carefully complete the table below. Jot down what



                                         PA G E 1 0 4
```
